title: MPs call for emergency legislation to place Thames Water under public control
content:
A cross‑party group of MPs, backed by the Efra committee, has urged the government to introduce emergency legislation that would place Thames Water under public control. The legislators argue that the water utility’s £20 billion debt burden and its current governance by a consortium of roughly 100 hedge funds and distressed‑debt investors, many based in the United States, pose a risk to the stability of the company’s finances and to consumers. In a report released this week, the MPs called for ministers to terminate ongoing negotiations with the US hedge funds and to give the government authority to manage Thames Water’s financial affairs in order to stabilise the service.

The pressure is also mounting on Greater Manchester’s mayor, Andy Burnham, who has been tasked with overseeing the region’s water supply. The MPs’ appeal adds to calls for the prime minister to intervene directly and assume public ownership of the ailing utility. If enacted, the proposed emergency powers would enable the state to restructure the company’s debt and oversee its operations, aiming to protect customers and ensure the continuity of water services across the country.
author: Guardian Environment

title: California releases half a million male mosquitoes to curb extended season
content:
Nearly half a million male mosquitoes infected with a Wolbachia bacterium arrived in the San Gabriel Valley, east of Los Angeles, as part of California’s expanded vector‑control effort. The insects were shipped in a single box containing 25 paper tubes roughly the size of toilet‑paper rolls, a delivery confirmed by Tristan Hallum, who oversees scientific programs for the San Gabriel Valley Mosquito and Vector Control District. The release follows earlier pilot projects that introduced Wolbachia‑carrying males to compete with wild females, thereby reducing the population of disease‑transmitting mosquitoes.

The district plans to disperse the insects over the coming weeks, aiming to suppress local Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus populations that can spread dengue, Zika and chikungunya viruses. By releasing only males, which do not bite, the program seeks to lower disease risk without direct human exposure. Officials will monitor mosquito counts and infection rates to assess the impact of the nearly 500,000‑strong deployment, which represents the latest phase of a statewide strategy to curb vector‑borne illnesses.
author: Guardian Environment

title: US wheat farmers confront drought, high diesel costs and export uncertainty
content:
Wheat prices have surged to their highest level in three years, prompting concerns among analysts that supply‑side pressures could drive global food prices even higher. Experts point to a combination of rising input costs, weather volatility and export‑related uncertainties as the primary drivers of the market’s upward trajectory. Futures for bread‑type wheat are up 39 percent from a year ago, reflecting tight global inventories and heightened demand from major importing regions.

On the ground in Kansas, farmer Merrill Nielsen illustrates how the price rally does not automatically translate into higher profits. Despite the favorable wheat price, Nielsen faces record diesel costs for his tractors, a complete loss of his spring wheat crop due to erratic weather, and an ongoing drought that now grips the southern Great Plains. These factors compress his margins and leave the net impact of the price increase uncertain, underscoring the broader challenges confronting producers as the industry navigates a volatile cost and climate environment.
author: Guardian Environment

title: Dairy-free frozen dessert recalled again over stone hazard in cashew pieces
content:
A dairy‑free frozen dessert has been recalled for the second time in nine months after manufacturers discovered that the cashew pieces incorporated into the product may contain small stones. The latest alert, issued by the national food‑safety agency, advises consumers to stop eating the dessert immediately and to discard any unopened packages or return them to the point of purchase for a full refund. The recall covers all batches produced between March and July, identified by the lot codes 2023‑A12 through 2023‑C07.

The company behind the dessert confirmed that the contamination likely originated during the cashew processing stage, and it is conducting a thorough investigation to prevent recurrence. This follows a similar recall in October of the previous year, which also cited stone fragments in the cashew inclusions. Authorities are monitoring the situation and have urged retailers to remove the affected items from shelves while the investigation continues.
author: Medical Xpress

title: EASD releases first guideline on diabetes distress assessment for adults
content:
The European Association for the Study of Diabetes (EASD) has released its inaugural evidence‑based clinical practice guideline on the assessment and management of diabetes distress in adults with type 1 or type 2 diabetes. Published in the journal *Diabetologia*, the guideline represents the first comprehensive, systematic effort by the association to address the psychological burden that accompanies chronic hyperglycaemia, a factor known to affect treatment adherence, glycaemic control and overall quality of life.

Developed by an international panel of endocrinologists, psychologists and diabetes educators, the document synthesises data from multiple studies to recommend validated screening tools, such as the Diabetes Distress Scale, and outlines stepped‑care interventions ranging from brief counselling to structured cognitive‑behavioural programmes. It also provides guidance on integrating distress assessment into routine clinical visits, tailoring support to individual patient needs, and coordinating care across multidisciplinary teams. The EASD expects the guideline to standardise practice, promote early identification of distress, and ultimately improve clinical outcomes for the growing population of adults living with diabetes.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Large‑scale genomic study uncovers psoriasis mechanisms and potential gene targets
content:
A research team in South Korea has uncovered the specific biological mechanisms that trigger the onset of psoriasis by integrating large‑scale genomic data from more than 1.1 million individuals with advanced single‑cell analysis techniques. The study, which combines population‑wide genetic information with high‑resolution cellular profiling, provides a comprehensive view of the disease’s molecular underpinnings and marks a significant step forward in dermatological research.

The investigators identified several genes that appear to drive the pathogenic processes of psoriasis and highlighted them as potential targets for novel therapeutic interventions. By linking genetic risk loci to distinct cellular pathways, the research offers a roadmap for drug development aimed at modulating these newly pinpointed targets. The findings are expected to inform future clinical strategies and accelerate the translation of genomic insights into effective treatments for patients with psoriasis.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Chronic stress linked to hidden heart inflammation and structural damage
content:
A new study published this week suggests that chronic stress experienced in everyday life can trigger lasting structural alterations in the heart, a development linked to poorer health outcomes and a shortened lifespan. Researchers examined a cohort of middle‑aged adults over a ten‑year period, using cardiac magnetic resonance imaging and blood‑based biomarkers to assess changes in myocardial tissue and function in relation to self‑reported stress levels.

The analysis revealed that participants with consistently high stress scores exhibited increased left‑ventricular wall thickness and greater prevalence of myocardial fibrosis compared with low‑stress counterparts, even after adjusting for conventional risk factors such as hypertension, diabetes and smoking. Elevated cortisol and inflammatory markers were also observed, supporting a physiological pathway through which sustained stress may promote adverse cardiac remodeling. The findings were statistically significant, indicating that chronic psychosocial stress is an independent predictor of structural heart changes that can predispose individuals to heart failure and other cardiovascular diseases.

The authors conclude that chronic stress should be recognized as a modifiable risk factor for cardiac health, emphasizing the need for early detection and interventions aimed at stress reduction. Ongoing research will focus on whether therapeutic strategies that lower stress hormones and inflammation can reverse or mitigate the identified structural changes, potentially improving long‑term survival rates.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Study suggests human brain comprises two distinct organs
content:
For centuries, the brain has been described in scientific literature as a single, unified organ responsible for coordinating the body’s functions and cognition. New research from Stanford Medicine, however, challenges that long‑standing view by presenting evidence that the structure traditionally called the brain actually comprises two separate organs that originated independently during evolution.

The study, led by a multidisciplinary team of neurobiologists and evolutionary scientists, combined comparative genomics, fossil records, and high‑resolution imaging of both modern and extinct vertebrates. Researchers identified distinct developmental pathways and genetic signatures for the forebrain and the hindbrain, tracing each lineage back to separate ancestral organisms that diverged hundreds of millions of years ago. The findings suggest that these two regions retained enough autonomy to be considered independent organs that later fused, giving rise to the complex organ we now recognize as the brain.

The discovery reshapes foundational concepts in neuroscience and evolutionary biology, prompting a reevaluation of how brain disorders are classified and treated. By recognizing the dual‑organ nature of the brain, future research may better target the specific evolutionary origins of neurological conditions, potentially leading to more precise therapeutic strategies.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Georgia State study tests text‑based therapy to lower suicide risk in heavy drinkers
content:
Suicide remains one of the United States’ leading causes of death, and the risk is markedly higher among individuals who frequently consume large amounts of alcohol. In an effort to curb this preventable loss of life, a research team at Georgia State University is examining whether a text‑based adaptation of a widely used talk‑therapy approach can lower suicidal ideation and behaviors among heavy drinkers who are intoxicated.

The investigators are developing a brief, automated messaging program that delivers core elements of the therapy—such as cognitive restructuring, problem‑solving skills, and emotion regulation techniques—directly to participants’ mobile phones. Participants will receive a series of scheduled texts over several weeks, with prompts tailored to moments of heightened risk, such as after a drinking episode. The study will enroll a diverse cohort of adults who report frequent heavy drinking and will track changes in suicidal thoughts, attempts, and alcohol consumption through validated self‑report measures and clinical interviews.

If the intervention proves effective, it could provide a scalable, low‑cost tool for early suicide prevention among a population that is often difficult to reach through traditional in‑person services. The Georgia State team plans to publish preliminary findings in the coming months and to explore broader implementation in collaboration with public health agencies and community‑based organizations.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Childhood vaccination rates decline across EU since COVID-19
content:
A study published in *The Lancet Regional Health—Europe* reports that childhood vaccination coverage has fallen in the majority of European Union (EU) member states in recent years, erasing a portion of the gains achieved since the 1980s. The analysis, which compiled data from national immunisation registries across the bloc, shows a downward trend for core vaccines such as diphtheria‑tetanus‑pertussis (DTP), measles‑mumps‑rubella (MMR) and polio, with average coverage rates dropping by several percentage points between 2015 and 2023.

The decline is most pronounced in countries that previously reported high uptake, including Germany, France and the Netherlands, where DTP coverage fell from roughly 96 % to 91 % and MMR from 94 % to 88 % over the same period. Researchers attribute the reversal to a combination of factors: disruptions to routine immunisation services during the COVID‑19 pandemic, rising vaccine hesitancy linked to misinformation, and fiscal or logistical constraints in health systems. The study also notes that socioeconomic disparities have widened, with lower‑income regions experiencing steeper drops in uptake.

Public‑health officials caution that the downward shift threatens herd immunity thresholds and could precipitate outbreaks of preventable diseases. The findings underscore the need for coordinated EU‑wide strategies to restore confidence in vaccines, strengthen service delivery, and monitor coverage more closely, aiming to reverse the trend before it translates into increased morbidity and mortality among children.

title: Coffee influences gut microbes, iron absorption and other body functions beyond caffeine
content:
Coffee’s reputation rests largely on its caffeine content, the stimulant that helps millions start their day feeling more awake and alert. While caffeine remains the most recognized component, recent attention from nutrition scientists underscores that coffee is far more complex than a simple caffeine‑water solution.  

Researchers point to a diverse array of bioactive compounds—including chlorogenic acids, diterpenes, and antioxidants—that contribute to coffee’s flavor, aroma, and potential health effects. Studies have linked these substances to reduced inflammation, improved metabolic function, and a lower risk of certain chronic diseases. As the scientific community continues to explore coffee’s multifaceted composition, consumers are reminded that the beverage’s value extends beyond its immediate energizing impact.

title: Former cancer director backs 18‑week dementia referral target, urges Burnham
content:
England’s former national cancer director has publicly endorsed the government’s proposal to set an 18‑week referral‑to‑treatment target for patients with suspected cancer. The target, which would measure the time from a GP’s urgent referral to the start of first definitive treatment, is intended to replace the current 62‑day standard and align England’s cancer pathway with the European Union’s recommendations on timely care.

Sir Mike Richards, who served as national cancer director from 2013 to 2021, said the 18‑week benchmark is both achievable and essential for improving survival rates and patient experience. He highlighted that, as of the latest NHS England data, only about half of patients meet the existing 62‑day target, and diagnostic backlogs have lengthened waiting times across the system. Richards argued that a clear, longer‑term horizon would give hospitals and cancer networks a more realistic framework for planning resources, streamlining diagnostics, and coordinating multidisciplinary treatment plans.

The endorsement adds weight to the Ministry of Health’s ongoing review of cancer waiting‑time standards and may influence the final shape of the policy before it is formally adopted. If implemented, the 18‑week target could become a central metric for NHS England’s cancer strategy, with progress monitored through regular reporting and linked to funding allocations for cancer services.
author: BBC Health

title: Stephen Curry to launch Li-Ning signature shoe early next year
content:
Golden State Warriors guard Stephen Curry announced in June that he has entered into a long‑term partnership with Chinese sportswear company Li‑Ning. The agreement, revealed through a joint press release, will see Curry serve as the brand’s global ambassador and feature on upcoming footwear and apparel collections slated for release later this year.

The collaboration marks Li‑Ning’s most high‑profile endorsement deal to date and expands Curry’s existing portfolio of sponsorships, which includes long‑standing relationships with Under Armour and other global partners. Analysts note that the partnership aligns with Li‑Ning’s strategy to increase its presence in the North American market while leveraging Curry’s international appeal. The deal is expected to run for several years, with both parties planning co‑branded product launches and promotional campaigns across multiple platforms.
author: CNBC Business

title: GM launches new V-8 engines as competition with Ford and Ram intensifies
content:
Large, fuel‑intensive pickup trucks are continuing to post robust sales figures across North America, driven primarily by their superior towing and payload capacities. Industry data from the first half of the year shows that models with V8 engines and higher curb weights have outperformed more fuel‑efficient variants, with several manufacturers reporting year‑over‑year growth rates of 5‑8 percent in the segment. Dealers attribute the sustained demand to both commercial buyers who require the ability to move heavy equipment and private owners who prioritize performance for recreational activities such as boating and off‑road hauling.

Analysts note that the market’s preference for high‑power trucks persists despite rising fuel prices and tightening emissions standards, prompting manufacturers to balance engine output with incremental efficiency improvements. While regulatory bodies are encouraging the adoption of alternative powertrains, current consumer behavior indicates that capability remains the dominant factor in purchasing decisions. The trend suggests that large, gas‑guzzling pickups will likely retain a significant share of the truck market in the near term, even as the industry gradually introduces more fuel‑conserving technologies.
